title: Myxoedema coma
subject: endocrinology
summary: Suspect in a hypothermic, drowsy patient with hypothyroidism and a precipitant; give stress-dose hydrocortisone and IV levothyroxine 200 to 400 mcg loading (100 to 200 mcg if older or cardiac), then 1.6 mcg/kg/day (75% if IV), with ICU supportive care and passive rewarming.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Decompensated severe hypothyroidism: altered mental state (lethargy for weeks, confusion, stupor, less often coma), hypothermia and multi-organ dysfunction. Most patients are not comatose; mortality may reach 50%.

Typical patient: older woman with known hypothyroidism (autoimmune, post-radioiodine or post-thyroidectomy) who stopped levothyroxine, with a precipitant: cold exposure, infection, stroke, MI, GI bleeding, sedatives, opioids, tranquillisers or diuretics.
Signs: hypothermia, hypoventilation, bradycardia, hypotension, dry coarse skin, macroglossia, periorbital oedema, delayed reflex relaxation, ileus, pericardial or pleural effusion.

Popoveniuc score (temperature, CNS, GI, precipitant, heart rate, effusions or hypotension, metabolic): 60 or more highly suggestive, 45 to 59 at risk, below 45 unlikely. Interpret with biochemistry; sepsis can score similarly.
Infection may present without fever, tachycardia or raised white cell count.

sections.title: Investigations
items: TSH and FT4 (TSH may be low or normal in central hypothyroidism); random cortisol (with ACTH if possible) drawn BEFORE hydrocortisone, without delaying it.
Sodium (hyponatraemia), glucose (hypoglycaemia), arterial gas (hypercapnia, hypoxaemia), CK, creatinine, CBC (macrocytic anaemia), lipids, blood and urine cultures.
ECG (bradycardia, low voltage, QT prolongation, block), chest X-ray, echocardiography for pericardial effusion; CT brain if focal signs.

sections.title: Immediate treatment (HDU or ICU)
items: Treat on clinical suspicion; do not wait for thyroid results. Secure the airway and assess ventilation: hypoventilation and hypercapnia often need non-invasive or mechanical ventilation.
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, then 50 mg IV every 6 hours (or 200 mg/24 hours by infusion) until adrenal insufficiency is excluded. Give it with, or before, thyroid hormone.
Levothyroxine IV loading dose 200 to 400 mcg; use 100 to 200 mcg in small or older patients and those with ischaemic heart disease or arrhythmia.
Then levothyroxine 1.6 mcg/kg/day (the oral replacement dose), given as 75% of that dose while IV (about 1.2 mcg/kg/day IV).

Liothyronine is optional and controversial: a pragmatic approach is levothyroxine alone for the first 24 hours, adding liothyronine 2.5 to 10 mcg every 8 hours only if not improving. Extreme caution in older adults and ischaemic heart disease.
Passive rewarming with blankets only; active external warming can cause vasodilatation and cardiovascular collapse.
Start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics after cultures until infection is excluded, and treat the precipitant.

sections.title: Supportive care
items: Hypotension: cautious IV crystalloid or blood; avoid fluid overload. Correct hyponatraemia cautiously with close sodium monitoring; avoid hypotonic fluids.
Hypoglycaemia is common: monitor capillary glucose and give dextrose infusion as needed.
Avoid sedatives and opioids where possible: drug clearance is reduced and they worsen hypoventilation.

Where IV levothyroxine is not available (common in Indian hospitals), start levothyroxine via nasogastric tube without delay, recognising that gut absorption is unreliable, and involve endocrinology urgently.

sections.title: Monitoring and step-down
items: Continuous ECG and BP monitoring for tachyarrhythmia or ischaemia after thyroid hormone; hourly temperature, GCS, glucose; frequent arterial gases and sodium.
FT4 (with FT3) on alternate days, aiming for FT4 in the middle of the reference range without excess FT3. TSH normalises slowly and should not guide early treatment.
Once cardiorespiratory status is stable, stop liothyronine (replace with levothyroxine) and switch to oral levothyroxine when fully conscious.
Stop hydrocortisone once the adrenal axis is cleared (pre-treatment cortisol, or 9 am cortisol or Synacthen test before the morning dose).
After stabilisation watch for AKI, GI bleeding and pulmonary haemorrhage.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Older adults and ischaemic heart disease: lower levothyroxine loading dose (100 to 200 mcg) and avoid or minimise liothyronine.
Central (pituitary) hypothyroidism: TSH is not raised and ACTH deficiency (secondary adrenal insufficiency) may coexist; give hydrocortisone before thyroid hormone.
Hypothyroidism after radioiodine or thyroidectomy for Graves disease is a common background; check adherence and supply before discharge.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving thyroid hormone without glucocorticoid cover, which can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Active external rewarming.
Attributing all findings to the thyroid and missing sepsis, stroke or electrolyte causes.
Too high a thyroid hormone dose in older or cardiac patients (arrhythmia, MI); too low a dose fails to reverse the crisis.

drugs.name: Levothyroxine IV
drugs.dose: Loading 200 to 400 mcg IV once (100 to 200 mcg if small, older, ischaemic heart disease or arrhythmia); then 1.6 mcg/kg/day reduced to 75% while IV
drugs.notes: Switch to oral once conscious and absorbing.

drugs.name: Liothyronine (T3)
drugs.notes: Alternative regimen: 10 to 25 mcg IV with a 200 to 300 mcg levothyroxine load, then 2.5 to 10 mcg IV every 8 hours. Lower doses in older or cardiac patients.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.dose: 100 mg IV immediately, then 50 mg IV every 6 hours (or 200 mg/24 hours by continuous infusion)
drugs.notes: Continue until adrenal insufficiency is excluded.

sources.title: Management of endocrine emergencies: joint consensus statement for management of myxoedema coma
Guidelines for the treatment of hypothyroidism: prepared by the ATA task force on thyroid hormone replacement
